clue.text: …high pass and a circuit around open country

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the circuit is wrapped about the open country

parts.note: a loop is a circuit
a ley, or lea, is open grassland

explanation.surface: Continuing from 26: a lofty mountain pass and a walking circuit round the open downland.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 26 across, making the surface a hiking trip, but 'high pass' is a lofted pass in basketball.
explanation.definitionFit: An alley-oop is a basketball move where the ball is lobbed high for a teammate to catch and dunk.

clue.text: City yearbook's choice of covers?

indicators.note: the covers of a book are its outside, front and back, and they enclose what lies between them

parts.note: the front and back covers of the word
or offers a choice between alternatives

explanation.surface: Asking which cover design a city's annual has chosen.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle's hidden message honours a York City footballer, so 'City' has a second, football sense too.
explanation.definitionFit: York is a historic cathedral city in North Yorkshire, England.

clue.text: The price of fish would be more relevant to Shaw in play!

definitions.text: The price of fish would be more relevant

indicators.note: something in play is moving freely about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A dismissive critic implying that a George Bernard Shaw drama is utterly beside the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's that got to do with the price of fish?' is a British retort to an irrelevant remark; the answer is a similar dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying so what dismisses a point as irrelevant, the same put-down as asking what it has to do with fish prices.

clue.text: American people love Frenchman's heart being worn on his sleeve

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only its middle letter is kept

parts.note: the central letter of the nine-letter word
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
manche is the French word for sleeve, the Frenchman's own

explanation.surface: A Frenchman wearing his heart on his sleeve, openly showing his love.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the first pieces sit 'on' the sleeve, above it. 'His' points back to the Frenchman, so the sleeve is in French.
explanation.definitionFit: The Comanche are a Native American nation of the southern Great Plains.

clue.text: Name development of Lakeside pre-eminently after US pop singer

indicators.note: a development changes the form of something, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name
part of the anagram fodder

indicators.note: pre-eminently is read as at the very front, so the following word gives only its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lakeside property development named in honour of an American pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like a link word placing the singer second; it supplies one letter to the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Sedaka is an American singer-songwriter known for hits such as Breaking Up Is Hard to Do.

clue.text: Still a fixture of theatre stalls

indicators.note: a fixture is something fixed inside a place, so the letters are found within the following words

parts.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: Something that remains a permanent feature of a theatre's seating area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb meaning yet; it is the adjective meaning motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at rest is not moving, which is what being still means.

clue.text: 'Colas' cheekily containing shot?

indicators.note: containing means holding something inside, so one piece sits within the other
doing something cheekily means taking liberties, so the word in quotes is treated irreverently and jumbled

parts.note: the quoted word is the anagram fodder
a pop is a shot or attempt, as in having a pop at something

explanation.surface: Fizzy drinks described with a wink as having a sneaky shot of spirits in them.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: alcopops are sweet soft drinks with alcohol added, colas with a shot in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcopops are bottled fizzy drinks pre-mixed with spirits, which is what a cola laced with a measure amounts to.

clue.text: Screw, perhaps, wrapping hands around lag's midriff

indicators.note: wrapping means enclosing on all sides, so the following pieces go inside

parts.note: say means perhaps, as in 'say, ten people'

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the hands flank the middle letter

parts.note: L and R, the left and right hands
the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: A prison officer, a screw, gripping a convict round the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' is British slang for a prison guard, which fits the lag, a convict; here it is old slang for wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Screw is dated British slang for wages or pay, the regular sum an employee receives.

clue.text: Have something to pay outspoken film heroine

indicators.note: outspoken means said out loud, so the phrase before it counts only by its sound

parts.note: to owe a debt is to have something to pay

explanation.surface: A borrower with bills due who also speaks their mind about a heroine on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: Odette (1950) is the film about the wartime agent Odette Sansom; the name is also the swan heroine of Swan Lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Odette is the title character of a 1950 British war film about a real secret agent.

clue.text: In the post, a bonus coffee pot

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a benefit that comes with a job, the post

explanation.surface: Finding a free coffee pot delivered in the mail as a pleasant extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' looks like the mail; it is a job, and the first definition is an extra that comes with employment.
explanation.definitionFit: A perk is a perquisite, an extra benefit of employment, and also informal shorthand for a percolator.

clue.text: False rocks fenced by lady in charge of racket, 50 per cent off?

indicators.note: being fenced by something means being enclosed within it, so one piece goes inside the other
something that rocks is shaken back and forth, so the preceding word is jumbled

parts.note: first part of Simona Halep, a Romanian tennis champion who wields a racket
the anagram fodder
rest of the tennis player's surname, closing around the jumbled letters

explanation.surface: A woman running a fraud racket, with fake gems involved, is only half switched on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' suggests crime, but the lady is HALEP, tennis star Simona Halep, wrapped around the jumbled letters. The question mark flags a playful definition: someone half asleep is 50 per cent 'off'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being drowsy and only partly awake is jokingly described as being half switched off, or 50 per cent asleep.

clue.text: A waste product rococo art used this to depict?

indicators.note: rococo art is florid and ornate, so the letters are elaborately rearranged
the letters of the solution plus the other two words together make up the definition phrase, so taking those two words away leaves this

parts.note: the definition phrase also supplies the full set of letters
these letters are removed from the full set

explanation.surface: An ornate eighteenth-century painting that, absurdly, used dung to portray dung.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a composite anagram: ART USED plus the answer, jumbled, spell A WASTE PRODUCT. 'This' stands for the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowpat is a flat dropping of cattle dung, a waste product of the animal.

clue.text: Go with a fresh essence

parts.note: go and pep both mean energy
a means per, as in five pounds a head
mint means brand new, as in mint condition

explanation.surface: Choosing an option with a new fragrance or flavouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' looks like an article; it stands for per, a rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Peppermint essence is a concentrated flavouring extract distilled from the mint plant.

clue.text: Uncommonly shaky painter of 2 resting on stack

parts.note: a rick is a stack of hay or straw
William Etty was a painter from York, the answer to 2 down

explanation.surface: An artist perched precariously on top of a haystack.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'resting on' puts the painter after the stack. 'Uncommonly' warns that this is the rarer spelling with a double T.
explanation.definitionFit: Rickety means unsteady and liable to collapse; the spelling with two Ts is a less usual variant.

clue.text: Unprincipled snapper on the case of your independent manuscripts

parts.note: a pap is a paparazzo, a press photographer known for having few scruples

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the outer letters of the word
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: A sleazy press photographer chasing an independent writer's private papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snapper' could be a fish or a dog; here it is a photographer, and 'unprincipled' describes the type rather than removing a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Papyri are ancient documents written on sheets made from reeds, so they are early manuscripts.

clue.text: Abdication, but not wanting son on the throne…

indicators.note: not wanting something means doing without it, so the named letter is dropped

parts.note: abdication is resigning from the crown
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A monarch giving up the crown but refusing to hand it to their son.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 18 down, which is built the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A reigning monarch is the one currently ruling, seated on the throne.

clue.text: Sport doctor's box is missing old powder case

indicators.note: the two letters spelling the word is are absent, so they are dropped from the end of the box's name

parts.note: PE is physical education, school sport
the TARDIS is the police-box time machine of Doctor Who

explanation.surface: A sports physician finds their kit box empty of an old container of gunpowder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is missing' reads as the box lacking something; it literally removes the letters IS from TARDIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A petard was a small bomb, a metal case packed with gunpowder used to blast through gates.

clue.text: …skilfully making plans, but not wanting son's act of condescension

indicators.note: not wanting something means doing without it, so the named letter is dropped

parts.note: designing is skilfully drawing up plans
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Continuing from 16: a scheming parent plotting cleverly while disowning the heir, a haughty gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Deigning is stooping to do something one considers beneath oneself, a gesture of condescension; the verbal noun matches 'act'.

clue.text: Do one's bit catching swallow

indicators.note: catching means seizing and holding, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
to swallow food is to eat

explanation.surface: Doing your part by catching a swallow, the bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do one' is British slang for clear off; ''s' stands for 'is'. 'Swallow' looks like the bird but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat it and do one are both rude slang commands telling someone to go away.

clue.text: Make novel Christmas break?

parts.note: surface reading: give the festive season a new twist
setter's reading: what must you do to the word novel to turn it into Noel? Remove the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Someone planning an unusual, original holiday season.
explanation.walkthrough: Take V, the Roman five, out of NOVEL and NOEL, Christmas, is left; the instruction itself is the answer, a phrase for a short break.
explanation.definitionFit: Take five is an informal instruction to pause for a few minutes' rest, a brief interval.

clue.text: Could this be Wembley Way?

parts.note: surface reading: the famous approach road to Wembley Stadium in London
setter's reading: split the answer one and five and it describes Wembley, the stadium, a sporting arena

explanation.walkthrough: Wembley Way is the road leading to Wembley Stadium, London's national football ground. Split, the answer reads as an article and a word for a stadium.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenue is a broad road or street, a kind of way.

clue.text: Shot No.1, position No.1?

parts.note: GO A is a first attempt, shot number one, with A as the first
to lie is to be positioned, as a golf ball lies

explanation.surface: A sports report noting the first strike and the top-ranked position.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'No.1' is wordplay giving A; the second, with its question mark, is the definition, since the keeper traditionally wears the number 1 shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: In football the goalkeeper is conventionally given shirt number one, so the keeper is the team's 'number one'.

clue.text: Periodically the one cloth that may be used to clean up gemstone?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, the other way round
periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters of the two words
a rag is a cloth for wiping

explanation.surface: A periodic reminder of the special cloth used to polish a precious stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Garnet is a deep red semi-precious mineral cut and polished as a jewel.

clue.text: Milestone parties most common in Hertfordshire market town

indicators.note: to party is to live it up wildly, so the preceding word's letters are thrown about

parts.note: the anagram fodder
this letter appears three times in the county name, more than any other

explanation.surface: Celebrations held on a landmark occasion in a typical Home Counties shopping town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hertfordshire market town' looks like the definition, but Leominster is in Herefordshire; Hertfordshire only supplies its most frequent letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Leominster is a small historic trading town in Herefordshire, in the West Midlands of England.

clue.text: Islanders like to?

parts.note: surface reading: people from an island who are fond of something
setter's reading: the word to is tom lacking its last letter, a tom being a cat, and the island's cats famously have no tails

explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is known for its tailless breed of cat; 'to' is a tom (cat) with its tail docked, so it is like one of these cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Manx is the adjective and collective name for the people of the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Waxer and Waner are demonstrably cheeky!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the satellite that grows and shrinks each month
second meaning: to bare one's bottom as a prank, showing one's cheeks

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'Waxer and Waner' look like a pair of people; the verb then reads as they bare their behinds.
explanation.definitionFit: The moon waxes and wanes through its phases, and to moon is to expose your buttocks as an insult.

clue.text: Become the thing to retire?

parts.note: to turn is to become, as milk turns sour
the in thing is what is fashionable

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether stepping down is now the fashionable move.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn in is an informal phrase for going to bed, and retiring also means going to bed at night.

clue.text: To see them, head to SE England and look right…

definitions.text: To see them, head to SE England and look right…

parts.note: surface reading: travel to the south-east of England, where these chalk hills lie
setter's reading: in the printed newspaper grid, the down clues sit on the right-hand side of the page

explanation.surface: Travel directions for a sightseer heading to the countryside of south-east England.
explanation.walkthrough: The North and South Downs are chalk hills in south-east England; the downs are also the down clues, printed to the right. The ellipsis runs on into 1 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Downs are the rolling grassy chalk uplands of southern England, also a pun on the down clues.
